en: The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Jewel Adornment Spoken by the Buddha, also known as the Chapter of Mahākāśyapa;
translated during the Jin Dynasty, the name of the Tripiṭaka Master is lost.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great [assembly].

The assembly of bhikṣus numbered eight thousand, and there were sixteen thousand bodhisattvas who had gathered here from various buddha-fields, all of whom were resolved upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva loses the prajñāpāramitā. What are these four?"
First, they do not honor the Dharma nor respect the Dharma teacher;
second, those who act as Dharma teachers are stingy and begrudge the Dharma;
third, those who wish to obtain the Dharma create obstacles for it, rebuking and treating others with contempt, and thus fail to preach the Dharma for them.
Fourth, being hateful, arrogant, conceited, self-important, praising oneself,
and disparaging others. Kāśyapa,
these are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva loses the prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva attains the prajñāpāramitā.
What are the four?
First, to honor the Dharma and respect the Dharma teacher;

second, to receive and hear the Dharma as it is taught and extensively explain it to others, with a mind free from attachment and seeking nothing for oneself, but for the sake of the *prajñāpāramitā*, relinquishing all wealth and possessions and seeking extensive learning as if one’s head were on fire;
third, having heard it, to receive and uphold it.
Fourth, practicing the Dharma without attachment to verbal expression. Kāśyapa,
these are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva attains the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
if a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will forget the bodhicitta. What are these four?
First, deceiving one's teachers, elders, and seniors;
second, falsely accusing others of having committed offenses when they have done no wrong;
third, disparaging and slandering those who follow the Mahāyāna.
The fourth is to have a deceitful and hypocritical mind,
lacking ultimate sincerity. Kāśyapa,
these are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva forgets the bodhicitta.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,

if a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, from the very moment of birth until reaching the site of enlightenment, the bodhisattva-mind will always be present before them and will never be forgotten or lost."
What are the four?
First, one would rather die than ever speak falsely;
second, one regards all bodhisattvas as the World-Honored One and proclaims their praises in the four directions.
Third, they are free from flattery and hypocrisy, their minds being most sincere;
fourth, they do not delight in the Lesser Vehicle.
These, Kāśyapa, are called [the four qualities].

If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, from their first birth until they reach the site of enlightenment, the bodhisattva-mind will always be present before them and shall never be forgotten or lost.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
if a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, wholesome qualities that have arisen will perish and wholesome qualities will not increase.
What are these four?
First, they study worldly scriptures with arrogance and pride;
second, they are greedily attached to wealth and property and frequently visit the royal court;
third, they are jealous and slander others.
The fourth is to hear the preaching of sutras never heard before and then slander them. Kāśyapa,
these are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva causes existing goodness to perish and prevents new goodness from increasing.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
if a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, their goodness will not decline and they will increase in wholesome qualities.
What are these four?
First, they delight in hearing the sublime Dharma and do not delight in hearing what is contrary to the Dharma; they take pleasure in the Bodhisattva’s treasury of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
Second, they humble their minds and do not treat sentient beings with arrogance.

Third, they are content with the Dharma and eliminate false pride; when others commit offenses, they neither regard them as such nor speak of their faults, nor do they seek out the shortcomings or errors of others.

Fourth, regarding those dharmas one does not know, one should not speak of them as right or wrong; rather, one should take the Tathāgata as witness, for the Tathāgata’s immeasurable realm accords with the faculties of sentient beings, and that which the Buddha has taught is something I am unable to fathom.
This is what is meant, Kāśyapa:
when a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, their goodness does not decline and they increase in wholesome qualities.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa:
The mind has four crookednesses that a bodhisattva should eliminate. What are the four?
First, being hesitant and doubtful regarding the Buddha-dharma.
Second, out of arrogance, one remains silent toward sentient beings who are angry;
third, one gives rise to a mind of stinginess regarding the benefits obtained by others;
fourth, one disparages and slanders, rather than praising, bodhisattvas.
"Kāśyapa, these are called the four crookednesses of the mind that a bodhisattva should eliminate.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa..."
Bodhisattvas have four characteristics that accord with [the path]. What are the four?
First, they confess whatever transgressions they have committed and do not conceal them, so that their minds are free from entanglement and defilement.
Second, even if one dies because of a mantra, one never violates the truth of the mantra.

Third, regarding what is spoken, there shall be no mutual subversion; even if subjected to all forms of encroachment, deception, abuse, contempt, beating, binding, or harm, one considers it all to be the result of one's own past karma, neither giving rise to anger toward others nor producing the fetters of affliction.
Fourth, one remains firmly established in non-belief of what others say, yet maintains ultimate faith in the Buddha-dharma without being swayed by it, because of internal purity.
This, Kāśyapa, is called the four concordant signs of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa:
Bodhisattvas have four evils. What are the four?
First, they are learned yet arrogant and deceitful; their conduct does not accord with the Dharma, and they do not follow instructions and admonitions.
Second, to distance oneself from the True Dharma, to show no respect for teachers and elders, and to fail to consume offerings made out of faith;
third, to lose precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and to receive offerings while in a state of delusion and confusion;
fourth, upon seeing a taming and wise Bodhisattva, to fail to show respect, becoming arrogant and treating them with contempt.
This is what is meant, Kāśyapa:
a bodhisattva has four evils.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa:
Bodhisattvas possess four kinds of wisdom:
first, hearing what has not been heard before and practicing in accordance with the Dharma;
second, relying on the meaning rather than on literary embellishment.

Third, to follow the teachings and precepts with virtuous speech, ensuring that all actions are wholesome, being filial and respectful toward teachers and elders, and receiving the offerings of the faithful while possessing the virtues of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
fourth, upon seeing a Bodhisattva who is self-controlled and possesses wisdom, to give rise to a mind of goodness and reverence.
These, Kāśyapa, are called the four knowledges of a bodhisattva. Furthermore, Kāśyapa:
Bodhisattvas have four kinds of deviations. What are the four?
First, to consider sentient beings as close and dear before fully understanding them is a deviation of a bodhisattva.
Second, it is a transgression for a bodhisattva to preach the subtle and sublime Buddha-dharma to sentient beings who are unable to endure or receive it.
Third, it is a transgression for a bodhisattva to preach the inferior vehicle to those who delight in the supreme and wondrous [teachings].
Fourth, while all sentient beings who practice correctly attain the sublime Dharma, they may act in mutual opposition; this constitutes a transgression on the part of the bodhisattva.
Thus it is said, Kāśyapa:
there are four such transgressions of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
there are four paths for a bodhisattva. What are the four?
First, to maintain an impartial mind toward all sentient beings;
second, to exhort all sentient beings to study the wisdom of the Buddha;
third, to preach the True Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
Fourth, to cause all sentient beings to accord with right practice.
Kāśyapa, these are called the four paths of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
there are four kinds of evil associates for a bodhisattva.
What are these four?
First, the śrāvakas benefit only themselves;
second, the pratyekabuddhas have little purpose and little activity;
third, the secular treatises of teachers are devoted solely to verbal eloquence.
The fourth is to practice with them and obtain only worldly dharmas, not attaining the true Dharma.
Kāśyapa, these are called the four evil spiritual friends of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
there are four kinds of spiritual friends for a bodhisattva.
What are these four?
Those who come to beg are the spiritual friends of a bodhisattva, for they nurture the Path;
those who act as Dharma-teachers are the spiritual friends of a bodhisattva, for they nurture the perfection of wisdom through extensive learning;
those who encourage one to leave the household life and study the Path are the virtuous spiritual friends of a bodhisattva, for they nurture all roots of goodness.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are the spiritual friends of bodhisattvas, for they nurture all the qualities of a Buddha.
Kāśyapa, these are called the four spiritual friends of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
there are four counterfeit bodhisattvas. What are the four?
First, seeking profit and not seeking merit;
second, seeking only one's own happiness and not acting for the sake of sentient beings;
third, removing only one's own suffering and not acting for the sake of sentient beings.
Fourth, desiring to have a retinue and not delighting in being separated from them.
Kāśyapa, these are called the four semblances of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
there are four kinds of true merit for a bodhisattva. What are the four?
First, understanding emptiness while believing in the retribution of actions;
second, understanding the absence of self while extending great compassion toward sentient beings;
third, though delighting in nirvāṇa, not abandoning the cycle of birth and death.
The fourth is to practice giving with the desire to transform sentient beings, without hoping for any recompense.
Kāśyapa, these are called the four true merits of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have four great treasuries. What are the four?
First, encountering the appearance of a Buddha in the world;
second, hearing the teaching of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā);
third, seeing the Dharma Master with a mind free from hindrance.
Fourth, to dwell joyfully in mountain forests with heedfulness.
Kāśyapa, these are called the four great treasuries of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva transcends all māras. What are these four?
First, not abandoning the bodhicitta;
second, having no mental obstruction toward any sentient beings;
third, being unstained by and unattached to any views.
The fourth is not to treat any sentient being with contempt or arrogance.
Kāśyapa, these are called the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva transcends all Māras.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva gathers and sustains all wholesome dharmas. What are these four?
First, they always dwell in mountain forests and marshes with minds free from deceit;
second, whether treated with kindness or unkindness, their minds are always patient and enduring;
third, they mindfully repay the four debts of gratitude, even sacrificing their own bodies and lives for the sake of sentient beings.
Fourth, seeking the Dharma without weariness or satiety, because of possessing all roots of goodness.
This, Kāśyapa, is called the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva gathers and sustains all goodness.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
there are four immeasurable meritorious practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are the four?
First, to practice the gift of Dharma with a mind free from expectation;
second, to give rise to great compassion upon seeing those who violate the precepts;
third, to vow that all sentient beings may delight in the bodhisattva mind.
Fourth, seeing those who are weak and inferior, one does not abandon patience.
These, Kāśyapa, are called the four immeasurable meritorious practices of a bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, one is not called a bodhisattva merely by virtue of the name 'bodhisattva. It is because of practicing the practice of Dharma, practicing equal conduct, and practicing the discernment of dhyāna that one is called a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who accomplishes thirty-two qualities is entitled to be called a 'bodhisattva. What are these thirty-two?
First, to benefit sentient beings with a sincere heart;
second, to desire to attain the wisdom of sarvajña;
third, to be self-effacing and not disparage the wisdom of others.
Fourth, not being arrogant toward any sentient beings;
fifth, having faith in all sentient beings;
sixth, cherishing and caring for all sentient beings.
Seventh, to have ultimate compassion for all sentient beings;
eighth, to maintain an impartial mind toward both enemies and kin;
ninth, when sentient beings seek nirvana, to benefit them with immeasurable merit.
Tenth, seeing sentient beings, he speaks to them with joy;
eleventh, having given his word, he has no regrets;
twelfth, his great compassion pervades all sentient beings.
Thirteenth, seeking the Dharma and hearing it much without weariness;
fourteenth, recognizing one's own transgressions as faults;
fifteenth, admonishing others when seeing them commit transgressions without becoming angry.
Sixteenth, practicing all modes of dignified conduct and etiquette;
seventeenth, giving without expecting recompense;
eighteenth, practicing patience without obstruction.
Nineteenth, to diligently seek all roots of goodness;
twentieth, to cultivate meditative concentration that transcends the formless realm;
twenty-first, to embrace wisdom through skillful means.
Twenty-second, employing the four ways of attracting others as skillful means;
twenty-third, regarding those with precepts and those without precepts equally with a compassionate mind;
twenty-fourth, listening to the Dharma with a sincere heart.
Twenty-fifth, he dwells exclusively in mountains and marshes;
twenty-sixth, he does not delight in worldly glory;
twenty-seventh, he does not delight in the Lesser Vehicle but delights in the merit of the Great Vehicle.
Twenty-eighth, distancing oneself from evil associates and associating with virtuous friends;
twenty-ninth, accomplishing the four Brahma-abodes;
thirtieth, relying upon wisdom.
Thirty-first, they never abandon sentient beings, whether those beings are practicing or not;
thirty-second, their speech is non-dual, they revere mantras, and the bodhisattva-mind is foremost.
This is what is meant, Kāśyapa:
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who accomplishes these thirty-two dharmas is entitled to be called a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa:
I shall now speak a parable for you; by means of a parable, the wise may come to know the merit of a bodhisattva.
For example, the element of earth is non-dual for all sentient beings; even so, Kāśyapa!
From the first generation of the resolve for enlightenment until reaching the site of awakening, the Bodhisattva acts for the sake of all sentient beings without duality.
It is just as the element of water produces the hundred grains, various medicines, grasses, and trees; even so, Kāśyapa!
The Bodhisattva, with a sincere and pure mind of compassion, nurtures all beings and gives rise to blue and white virtues for the sake of all sentient beings.
It is like the element of fire that ripens the hundred grains, medicinal herbs, and plants; even so, Kāśyapa!
By means of the Prajñāpāramitā, the Bodhisattva brings all sentient beings to fulfillment.
Just as the element of wind adorns all Buddha-fields, so it is, Kāśyapa!
The Bodhisattva adorns all Buddha-lands through skillful means (upāya-kauśalya).
Just as the moon waxes day by day, so it is, Kāśyapa!
The Bodhisattva is sincere and pure, increasing all wholesome and pure dharmas.
Just as the rising sun illuminates all sentient beings;
so it is, Kāśyapa!
The Bodhisattva, by means of the perfection of prajñā, illuminates all sentient beings.
Just as the lion, king of deer, has no fear whatsoever wherever he goes;
so it is, Kāśyapa!
When a bodhisattva abides in the merit of ethical discipline, they are entirely free from fear and dread in whatever they do.
Just as a king of elephants can bear all manner of heavy burdens without ever becoming weary or fatigued; even so, Kāśyapa!
The Bodhisattva skillfully disciplines the mind, bearing the heavy burden for the sake of all sentient beings without weariness or fatigue.
Just as a lotus flower grows in the mud yet is not defiled by water;
so too does the Bodhisattva arise in the world yet remains unattached to worldly dharmas.
It is like cutting down a tree: although its branches are severed, if the root is not uprooted, it will grow back as before.
In the same way, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva, through the mind of skillful means, may sever the fetters of bondage yet still manifest within the triple world.
For example, just as the waters of the rivers from all directions, once they enter the great ocean, become of a single flavor;
so it is, Kāśyapa!
Whatever various kinds of meritorious vows and deeds a bodhisattva performs, when they attain the path of Buddhahood, they all become of a single flavor.
Just as the Four Heavenly Kings and the Gods of the Thirty-three Heavens dwell upon Mount Sumeru,
so too, Kāśyapa, do the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva abide within their mind.
Just as a king’s affairs of state are fully accomplished through the assistance of his ministers, so too, Kāśyapa,
are all the buddha-activities fully accomplished by a bodhisattva through the assistance of the roots of goodness of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
For example, Kāśyapa!
Just as rain cannot be obtained when there are no clouds in the sky,
so too the rain of Dharma cannot be obtained by a bodhisattva who has not heard much.
For example, Kāśyapa!
Just as when there are clouds in the sky, rain and moisture can be obtained;
so it is with the Bodhisattva, who possesses the great cloud of loving-kindness capable of bringing down the rain of the Dharma.
Just as the seven treasures can be obtained when a noble cakravartin king appears;
so too, Kāśyapa, when a bodhisattva appears,
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment— the jewels of the Path— can be obtained.
For example, Kaśyapa, just as one who possesses a maṇi jewel can obtain all manner of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kinds of gems therein; so too, Kaśyapa,
for one who possesses the bodhisattva-mind, all manner of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of dharmas of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can be obtained therein.
For example, when the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three roam through the Caitraratha Grove, all their articles of pleasure are entirely equal; so it is, Kāśyapa!
When a bodhisattva is sincere and pure, they employ skillful means equally for all sentient beings, without any distinction or gradation whatsoever.
Just as poison cannot cause harm due to the presence of medicinal mantras, so it is,
Kāśyapa: the poison of a bodhisattva’s afflictions cannot cause harm due to the presence of the medicine of wisdom.
For example, just as the manure and soil in a city or town are of great benefit for the use of fields;
so it is, Kāśyapa, that a bodhisattva,
by means of the fetters, trains for the sake of the use of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
Therefore, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva who wishes to study this *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* should correctly contemplate all phenomena.
What is meant by "correct contemplation"?
It refers to the true contemplation of all phenomena.
What is meant by the true contemplation of all phenomena?
It means not contemplating a self, a person, or a life-span; this is called the Middle Way, the true contemplation of phenomena.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, as for the true contemplation:

it means not contemplating that form is permanent or impermanent, nor contemplating that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are permanent or impermanent; this is called the Middle Way, the dharma of true contemplation."
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, what is the true contemplation of all phenomena?

It means not contemplating whether the earth element is permanent or impermanent, nor contemplating whether the elements of water, fire, and wind are permanent or impermanent; this is called the Middle Way, the true contemplation of phenomena.

"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, permanence is one extreme and impermanence is the second extreme. Between these two, there is no form; it is invisible and unattainable. This is called the Middle Way, the true contemplation of the Dharma."

To hold that there is a self is one extreme; to hold that there is no self is the second extreme. Between these two is that which is formless, invisible, and ungraspable; this is called the Middle Way, the true method of contemplation.

To have a mind of reality is one extreme; to have no mind of reality is the second extreme. That which is without mind, without thought, without volition, and without consciousness—this is called the Middle Way, the true method of contemplation.
Thus, unwholesome phenomena, worldly phenomena, phenomena associated with contention, out-flowing phenomena, conditioned phenomena, and defiled phenomena—these are called one extreme.

Likewise, wholesome phenomena, supramundane phenomena, phenomena free from contention, non-out-flowing phenomena, unconditioned phenomena, and pure, bright phenomena—these are the second extreme. Between these two, there is nothing whatsoever that can be apprehended; this is called the Middle Way, the true method of contemplation.

Existence is one extreme; non-existence is the second extreme. Between these two, there is nothing whatsoever and nothing can be apprehended; this is called the Middle Way, the true method of contemplation.

"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, I shall explain to you: conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations; conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness are name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is clinging; conditioned by clinging is existence; conditioned by existence is birth; and conditioned by birth arise old age, death, suffering, affliction, grief, lamentation, and despair. In this way, this great mass of suffering arises."

When ignorance is exhausted, volitional formations are exhausted; when volitional formations are exhausted, consciousness is exhausted; when consciousness is exhausted, name-and-form are exhausted; when name-and-form are exhausted, the six sense bases are exhausted; when the six sense bases are exhausted, contact is exhausted; when contact is exhausted, feeling is exhausted; when feeling is exhausted, craving is exhausted; when craving is exhausted, clinging is exhausted; when clinging is exhausted, existence is exhausted; when existence is exhausted, birth is exhausted; when birth is exhausted, old age, death, suffering, affliction, grief, and lamentation are all exhausted. In this way, the great mass of suffering is extinguished.
There are neither these two, nor are there two modes of practice; that which can be known in between is called the Middle Way, the true method of contemplation.

When such practices are exhausted—namely, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age and death—there are neither these two, nor are there two modes of practice; that which can be known in between is [the Middle Way].
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!
This is called the Middle Way, the true contemplation of all phenomena.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa:
One who contemplates all phenomena through the true Middle Way does not contemplate all phenomena as empty by means of the samādhi of emptiness, because all phenomena are themselves empty.
One does not contemplate all phenomena as signless by means of the samādhi of signlessness, because all phenomena are themselves signless.
One does not contemplate all phenomena as wishless by means of the wishless samādhi, because all phenomena are themselves wishless.
One does not contemplate all phenomena as signless by means of the signless [samādhi], because all phenomena are themselves signless.
One does not contemplate the non-arising of all phenomena by means of non-arising, because all phenomena are themselves without arising.
One does not contemplate the non-birth of all phenomena by means of non-birth, because all phenomena are themselves without birth.
One does not contemplate the suchness of all phenomena by means of suchness, because all phenomena are themselves such.
This is called the Middle Way’s true contemplation of phenomena.
One does not contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena by means of a non-existent person, because all phenomena are themselves empty.
Thus, the beginning is empty, the end is empty, and the present world is empty. You should cause them to rely upon emptiness and not rely upon persons.
If there are those who rely upon emptiness and depend on this emptiness, I say that such persons are far removed from this Dharma.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!

It would be better to rely on a view of self as vast as Mount Sumeru than for one who is not free from arrogance and lacks extensive learning to rely on a view of emptiness; such a person is beyond my care.

Suppose, for example, a skilled physician administers medicine according to the illness; once the illness has been eliminated, the medicine remains. In your view, Kāśyapa, would the person’s suffering and affliction be completely ended?
He replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
"Why is that? Because the medicine remains within the body.
It is even so, Kāśyapa!"
Emptiness cuts off all views; if there are those who rely on the view of emptiness, I do not treat them, and it is likewise so.
It is like a person who, fearing empty space, weeps and says:
"Now you must remove this empty space for me!"
"Kāśyapa, what do you think? Would he be able to go? He replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
‘It is so, Kāśyapa! If one fears emptiness, I say that such a person is utterly deluded.’”
Why is this? It is because sentient beings create emptiness and yet fear it.
It is like a painter who, having created an image of a ghost or spirit, becomes terrified by it himself.
In this way, Kāśyapa!

It is just so with all foolish commoners who create for themselves the phenomena of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch; they revolve through birth and death, remaining ignorant of these very phenomena.
For example, it is like a magician who creates an illusory person that then devours the magician;

there is nothing real about it. In the same way, Kāśyapa, when a practicing bhikṣu contemplates anything whatsoever, he finds it to be entirely deceptive, unreal, and lacking any solidity; it is just like this.
For example, just as two pieces of wood give rise to fire through their friction and then burn those very pieces of wood,
so too, Kāśyapa, it is the same:
the root of untainted wisdom arises because of the contemplation of reality, and that very contemplation of reality is then consumed by it.

For example, when a lamp is lit, all darkness is dispelled; yet this darkness comes from nowhere and goes nowhere—it does not come from the east, south, west, or north, nor does it go to those directions.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!
When wisdom has arisen, ignorance is extinguished; this ignorance comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
In this way, Kāśyapa,
the lamp has no such thought:
"I shall dispel the darkness."
"Yet when a lamp is lit, all darkness is immediately dispelled; both the lamp and the darkness are empty, ungraspable, without action, and without creation—it is just like this.
For example, Kāśyapa!"
If a hundred-year-old dark room were to have a lamp lit within it,
would that darkness ever think: "I shall remain here and not depart"?
He replied: “No, World-Honored One.”
"This darkness will surely be extinguished. "In the same way, Kāśyapa!

If there are sentient beings who have committed karmic formations and afflictions throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they can likewise be completely eliminated by the lamp of untainted wisdom of a single right contemplation."
Just as the five grains do not grow in the sky, so it is with the Bodhisattva:
the Buddha-dharma does not arise from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Just as the five grains grow upon the great earth, which is intermingled with all manner of impurities;
In this way, for a bodhisattva, the Buddha-dharma arises from within the midst of worldly entanglements and fetters.
It is like a lotus flower not growing on dry land;
likewise, for a bodhisattva, the Buddha-dharma does not arise from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Just as various lotuses grow from water in the mud;
so it is with the Bodhisattva, who gives rise to the Buddha-dharma from within the fetters of sentient beings who follow what is false.
It is like the finest clarified butter (sarpis) filling the four oceans.
One should know that the cultivation of roots of goodness by a bodhisattva is also like this.
For example, if a single hair were split into one hundred parts, and with one part of that hair one were to take a single drop of water from one of the four great oceans;
one should know that the cultivation of roots of goodness by a śrāvaka is also like this.
For example, Kāśyapa, it is like the hollow space within a mustard seed;
you should know that the cultivation of roots of goodness by śrāvakas is likewise so.
Just as the empty space of the ten directions is infinite,
one should know that the cultivation of roots of goodness by a bodhisattva is likewise so.
It is like when a queen of a Kṣatriya king born from the crown of his head has intercourse with a lowly man, and subsequently gives birth to a son.
"What do you think?
Should this son be called a prince? He replied:
"No, World-Honored One. "It is so, Kāśyapa!"
"These śrāvakas are born from my dharma-realm, yet none of them are the sons of the World-Honored One.
For example, suppose the great king Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja were to consort with a low-caste woman; if a son were later born to them, what do you think?"
"Since he was born of a lowly woman, should one not say that this son is not a prince? He replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
This is the prince. “It is so, Kāśyapa!”

Although born of lowly origins, he is nonetheless a prince; likewise, the Bodhisattva, having first resolved upon the mind of enlightenment, dwells within birth and death to teach and transform sentient beings, and all such beings are the sons of the Tathāgata.

For example, even though a noble wheel-turning monarch may have a thousand sons, if they lack the marks of a noble monarch, the monarch’s mind conceives the thought that he has no son. In the same way, Kāśyapa,
although the Tathāgata may have a multitude of hundreds of thousands of śrāvaka disciples, if there is no bodhisattva among them, the Tathāgata’s mind conceives the thought that he has no son.

For example, Kāśyapa, when the queen of a noble cakravartin king observes the fast for seven days, she gives birth to a boy endowed with the marks of a noble cakravartin; the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven all join in praising him, yet they do not mention the other great ones.
Why is this? Although the youth is small, he does not sever the lineage of the noble kings.

In the same way, when a bodhisattva first gives rise to the mind of enlightenment, even though his faculties are not yet fully developed, all those hosts of devas who have previously seen a Buddha will together praise him, rather than extolling the arhats who possess the eight liberations.
Why is this? Although they have only recently resolved to attain bodhicitta and their faculties are not yet fully developed, they do not sever the lineage of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
It is like a small maṇi pearl, which surpasses a crystal as large as Mount Sumeru.
In this way, when a bodhisattva first gives rise to the mind of enlightenment, they surpass all śrāvakas.
For example, Kāśyapa,
when the son of a noble wheel-turning monarch is first born, all his ministers and subjects pay him homage.
So it is with the Bodhisattva: when they first resolve their mind upon the Way, all devas and humans pay them homage.
Just as Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, produces various excellent medicines to treat the ailments and sufferings of all people without partiality or favoritism;
so it is with the Bodhisattva: they study the medicine of wisdom to treat the suffering of birth and death for all people, likewise without partiality or favoritism.
For example, one pays homage to the newly risen moon rather than to the later full moon;
even so, Kāśyapa, it is superior to pay homage to a bodhisattva who has first resolved for enlightenment than to one who has already attained the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Why is this? Because all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, are born from Bodhisattvas.
It is, for example, like this, Kāśyapa!
There is no one who would abandon the moon to pay homage to the stars;
likewise, there is no one who would abandon a bodhisattva endowed with full precepts, virtue, and wisdom to pay homage to a śrāvaka.
It is just so, Kāśyapa!
Just as no deva or human can turn rock crystal into a maṇi-jewel or pearl, so it is with the śrāvaka:
though they have accomplished all pure conduct of the precepts, they cannot sit beneath the Bodhi tree and attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
For example, just as one who obtains a genuine mani pearl acquires countless hundreds of thousands of other treasures, so it is with a Bodhisattva:
when such a being appears in the world, there likewise appear immeasurable śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas in the world.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, saying:

“For the sake of all sentient beings, the bodhisattva seeks to cultivate all roots of goodness and prepares a multitude of medicinal wisdoms; he travels to the four quarters and treats each according to their illness as it truly requires.”
Kāśyapa! What is treatment according to reality?
It means treating desire with the contemplation of foulness and impurity, treating hatred with a mind of loving-kindness, and treating delusion by means of dependent origination.

Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) remedies all views; signlessness (*animitta*) remedies all four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) remedies all [defilements] of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

The four non-perversions remedy all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) associated with the four perversions: impermanence remedies the perception of permanence in what is impermanent; suffering remedies the perception of pleasure in what is suffering; non-self remedies the perception of self in what is non-self; and the perception of impurity remedies the perception of purity in what is impure.

The four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni) are the remedies for attachment to the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena. In the contemplation of the body as body, one does not give rise to the view of a self in the body; in the contemplation of feelings as feelings, one does not give rise to the view of a self in feelings; in the contemplation of the mind as mind, one does not give rise to the view of a self in the mind; and in the contemplation of phenomena as phenomena, one does not give rise to the view of a self in phenomena.
The four right efforts consist in completely severing all unwholesome dharmas and cultivating all wholesome dharmas.
The four bases of psychic power consist in relinquishing the false conceptions of body and mind.
The five faculties and the five powers remedy lack of faith, indolence, distracted mindfulness, and ignorance.
The seven factors of enlightenment remedy ignorance regarding all phenomena.
As for the noble eightfold path, this wisdom remedies all false paths.
This, Kāśyapa, is called treating according to what is appropriate for each illness as it truly is.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!
A bodhisattva should train in this way.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
suppose all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm were like Jīvaka, the King of Physicians."
Someone asked him,
"By what method or medicine do you treat those who are ill?
He was ultimately unable to answer, for only a Bodhisattva can fully answer such a question.
Therefore, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva should form this thought:
"I should not seek mundane medicine; I should seek supramundane medicine."
"Cultivating all roots of goodness is the medicine of manifold wisdom.
One travels to the four quarters and treats the illnesses of sentient beings according to reality as they arise.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!"
What is the medicine of supramundane wisdom?

It is the wisdom of causes and conditions, and the wisdom of the non-existence of self, person, or life-span; it is the mind that understands all phenomena as empty and free from fear. One who practices such contemplation asks: "What is this desire of the mind?"
What is anger and delusion?
Are they of the past,
or are they of the future or the present?
If it is the past, the mind that has departed has already ceased;
if it is the future, the mind yet to come has not arisen;
if it is the present, the present mind does not abide.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!
The mind does not come from the future; it is not within, nor is it without, nor is it in between the two.
The mind is not form and is invisible; it is without resistance, without sight, without cognition, without abiding, and without further dependence.

Kāśyapa! As for the mind, all Buddhas have not seen it in the past, shall not see it in the future, and do not see it in the present. If all Buddhas have not seen it in the past, shall not see it in the future, and do not see it in the present, how can one know that there is anything practiced?
It is solely due to inverted perceptions that the activities of all phenomena exist.
All phenomena are like illusory transformations, for they undergo various births; this mind is like the wind, traveling far and impossible to grasp;
it is like flowing water, for it cannot remain still.
The mind is like the flame of a lamp, because it continues through a succession of conditions;
the mind is like a flash of lightning, because it does not abide for even a moment;
this mind is like mist, because external phenomena are defiled.
The mind is like a monkey, for it craves all sensory objects;
the mind is like a painter, for it creates various types of karmic formations;
the mind cannot remain still, for it follows along with the various fetters.
The mind is solitary and without companion, for it constantly delights in running about;
this mind is like a king, for it is the head of all phenomena;
this mind is like a mother, for it gives birth to all suffering.
This mind is like a flame, for it gathers and scatters all roots of goodness;
this mind is like a fishhook, for it conceives the notion of pleasure within suffering;
this mind is like a dream, for it conceives the notion of self within what is non-self.
This mind is like a fly, for it perceives purity in what is impure;
this mind is like an enemy, for it opposes what ought to be done within the household;
this mind is like a rākṣasa, for it constantly delights in seeking opportunities for harm.
This mind is like hatred and jealousy, for it constantly delights in seeking out faults;
this mind is not to be cherished, for it is deluded by attachment and craving;
this mind is like a thief, for it cuts off all roots of goodness.
This mind clings to forms, like a moth throwing itself into a flame;
this mind craves sounds, like the sound of military music and battle drums;
this mind craves fragrances, like a pig delighting in foul odors.
This mind is attached to flavors, just as a servant delights in leftover food;
this mind craves further pleasure, just as a fly delights in the scent of carrion.
When sought, the mind does not exist and cannot be found.
If there were nothing that could not be apprehended, then there would be no past, future, or present;
if there were no past, future, or present, then one would transcend the three periods of time;
and if one transcends the three periods of time, then one neither exists nor does one not exist.
If it is neither existent nor non-existent, this is non-arising;
if there is no arising, this is the absence of intrinsic nature;
if there is no intrinsic nature, this is the absence of origination.
If there is no arising, there is also no cessation;
if there is no cessation, then there is no decay;
if there is no decay, then there is neither coming nor going.
If there is no coming or going, then there is no birth and death;
if there is no coming and going and no birth and death, then there is no conditioned activity;
if there is no conditioned activity, then it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
If it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), then it is the nature of the sages and worthies;
if it is the nature of the sages, then there is neither precept nor non-precept;
if there is neither precept nor non-precept, then there is neither majestic deportment nor lack of majestic deportment.
If there were no volitional formations and no modes of deportment—neither proper nor improper deportment—then there would be no mind and no mental factors;
if there were no mind and no mental factors, then there would be no karma and no retribution;
and if there were no retribution, then there would be neither suffering nor pleasure.
If there were neither suffering nor pleasure, that would be the nature of the noble ones;
if it were the nature of the noble ones, then there would be no karma and no volitional action.
Within such a nature, there would be no performance of bodily karma, nor any performance of vocal or mental karma.
This nature is equal, without superior, middling, or inferior, and is likewise without distinction, for all dharmas are entirely equal.
"Thus it is, Kāśyapa!"
This nature is detached, for it relinquishes body and speech;
this nature is unconditioned, for it accords with nirvāṇa;
this nature is pure, for it is free from all fetters and defilements.
This nature is selfless, for it is free from the activity of a self;
this nature is impartial, for it is free from the distinction between the false and the real;
this nature is truly emergent, for it is essential to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This nature is inexhaustible, for it never arises and is eternally in accordance with the Dharma;
this nature delights in the unconditioned, for it is entirely equal;
this nature is pure, for it is ultimately without defilement.
"This nature is not the self, for a self cannot be found upon seeking it;
this nature is pure and white, because it is ultimately stainless. You, Kāśyapa!"
One should seek within, yet instead one seeks without.
In a future age, there will be bhikṣus who run about like dogs.
In what way do these bhikṣus run about like dogs?
It is like a dog that, when struck and thrown something to frighten it, runs back to chase after the object rather than toward the one who threw it.

In the same way, Kāśyapa, there will be śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who fear forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena, yet they instead take pleasure in them and do not examine within. Not knowing by what means they might become free from forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena, and remaining unaware, they eventually enter among human beings, where forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena once again find an opportunity to ensnare them.

Those who pass away while dwelling in mountains or marshes may, by virtue of observing worldly precepts, attain birth among the devas; yet they are subsequently overcome by the celestial objects of form, sound, fragrance, flavor, touch, and mental phenomena, and upon the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they are reborn in the four evil destinies.
What are the four?
They are among the denizens of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and asuras.
These, Kāśyapa, are what I call them.
A monk who runs about is just like a dog.
How is it that a monk does not run about like a dog?
If someone strikes or reviles him, he accepts it silently and does not retaliate.
When rebuked or provoked to anger, a bhikṣu does not retaliate with wrath; he merely contemplates his own body: "Who is it that reviles?
Who is it that strikes?
Who is it that experiences this resentment?"
This is what is meant, Kāśyapa:
such a bhikṣu does not run away like a dog.
He is like a charioteer who, when a horse becomes unruly, is able to restrain it.
The practicing bhikṣu is also like this: if the mind wanders and scatters, he immediately restrains it, causing it to follow [the path] without disorder.
It is like strangling a person; their life must necessarily be cut off.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!
All views that involve the conception of a self will inevitably sever the life-force of wisdom.
It is like a person who, according to whatever binds them, completely releases themselves from those bonds.
"In this way, monks, whatever binds the mind should be immediately removed.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa: for one who has left the household life to study the Path, there are two heavy fetters."
What are these two?
First, studying worldly scriptures;
second, carrying the robes and alms bowl without being diligent.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
there are two firm fetters for those who have left the household life to study the Path. What are these two?
First, the bondage of views;
second, the bondage of craving for wealth and reputation.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa:
There are two things that constitute obstacles for one who has left the household life to study the Way. What are these two?
First, associating intimately with laypeople.
Second, harboring resentment and jealousy toward teachers and friends.
Furthermore, there are two defilements for those who have left the household life to study. What are these two?
First, to take up any two of the fetters at will;
second, to go to the homes of acquaintances to beg for food.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!..."
There are two kinds of hailstorms for those who have left the household life to study the Way. What are the two?
First, slandering the True Dharma; [the second is...]
Second, they violate the precepts yet consume the offerings of the faithful.
Furthermore, there are two sores for those who have left the household life to study. What are these two?
First, observing the shortcomings of others;
second, concealing one's own shortcomings.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
Those who have left the household life and study possess two kinds of feverish distress. What are these two?
First, concealing impurity while wearing the kāṣāya.
Second, they desire that those who observe the precepts and practice follow and submit to them.
Furthermore, there are two ailments among those who have left the household life to study. What are these two?
First, they are arrogant and do not examine their own minds;
second, they revile those who study the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa:
Regarding the statement "a śramaṇa speaks of śramaṇas," how does a śramaṇa speak of śramaṇas?
There are four types of śramaṇas. What are the four?
First, the śramaṇa in appearance;
second, the śramaṇa of feigned deportment;
third, the śramaṇa of reputation.
The fourth is the true śramaṇa. What is a śramaṇa in appearance?

If there is a śramaṇa who possesses the outward appearance—having shaved off his hair and beard, donned the dharma robes, and holding the alms bowl—but whose bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and mental conduct are evil; who does not practice self-restraint nor guard his senses; who violates the precepts, commits evil, is greedy, and lacks diligence—this, Kāśyapa, is called a śramaṇa in appearance.
The semblance of a śramaṇa. What is a śramaṇa who feigns dignified deportment?

It refers to a śramaṇa who accomplishes the rules of etiquette, walks with right mindfulness, knows moderation in eating, and practices the four noble lineages; he does not delight in assemblies of the laity or the monastic community, speaks little, and sleeps little. Yet his deportment is falsely assumed and not genuine; he does not aspire for a pure mind, nor does he practice cessation and tranquility, yet he maintains views and conceptions. Regarding emptiness, he gives rise to the perception of it as a pit; toward those bhikṣus who practice emptiness, he conceives the notion of them being enemies. This, Kāśyapa, is called [the semblance of a śramaṇa].
Regarding the sham śramaṇa who feigns dignified deportment:
what is meant by a śramaṇa of reputation?
It refers to a śramaṇa who upholds the prohibitive precepts while desiring that others know he upholds them.
To diligently study with the desire to make others know of one's diligent study;
to dwell among mountains and marshes with the desire to make others know of one's dwelling in mountains and marshes;

to have few desires, be content, and dwell alone with diligence, desiring to make others know this; to never grow weary until death, not seeking the departure from desire, not delighting in cessation, not seeking the Way, and practicing the holy life with a stilled mind not for the sake of Nirvāṇa—this, Kāśyapa, is what is meant.
Regarding the "renowned śramaṇa": what is a "true śramaṇa"?

If there is a śramaṇa who does not act for the sake of his own body or life, much less out of greed for wealth or attachment to fame, who delights in hearing the Dharma of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and who, upon hearing it, rejoices and practices according to the Dharma—not practicing the holy life for the sake of nirvāṇa, much less for the sake of the three realms—[he is a true śramaṇa].
One does not form the view of emptiness, much less the views of a self, a person, or a life-span.

Seeking the Way according to the Dharma, one remains free from fetters and liberated, seeking no external paths. One contemplates that the nature of all dharmas is ultimately pure and stainless, and thus examines oneself through self-illumination rather than relying on others.

One who acts in accordance with the Dharma does not perceive a Tathāgata, much less a physical body; does not perceive the dharma of desirelessness, much less external ornamentation; does not conceptualize the unconditioned, much less a multitude of virtues; does not practice the dharma of cessation, nor study the dharma of cultivation; does not dwell in saṃsāra, nor delight in nirvāṇa; seeks neither liberation nor bondage. Knowing that all dharmas are ultimately pure, neither arising nor ceasing—this, Kāśyapa, is called... [the one who acts in accordance with the Dharma].
He is a true śramaṇa.
Therefore, Kāśyapa, you should train as a true śramaṇa; do not associate with those who are śramaṇas in name only.
"It is like a poor person who has the name 'rich' outside [of himself]. What do you think?
Does that name have any reality? He replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
‘It is so, Kāśyapa! There are those who have the name of a śramaṇa but lack the virtues of a śramaṇa; I say that such a person is utterly destitute.’”
For example, it is like a person who, while being swept away by a great flood, dies of thirst;

even so, Kāśyapa, there are śramaṇas and brahmins who study many teachings, yet are unable to eliminate the thirst of lust, anger, and delusion. They are swept away by the waters of the Dharma and die of the thirst of their fetters, being reborn in evil destinies—this is exactly the same.
"Kāśyapa, it is just as a physician who carries various medicines to treat the illnesses of others but does not treat his own;
likewise, Kāśyapa,
there are śramaṇas and brahmins who recite the Dharma extensively but do not eliminate their own diseases of lust, anger, and delusion— it is exactly like this."
"Suppose, for example, a sick person takes a king’s excellent medicine, yet fails to regulate his own conduct and consequently dies;
even so, Kāśyapa, many śramaṇas and brahmins act contrary to the Dharma and give rise to the diseases of the fetters (saṃyojana), and thus at the end they are born in evil destinies— just like that."
For example, just as a mani jewel that falls into impurity has no further value;
so it is, Kāśyapa! When many śramaṇas and brahmins are greedily attached to wealth and profit, you should know that they are likewise like a mani jewel fallen into impurity, having no further value.
It is, for example, like a dead man wearing a garland of golden flowers; even so, Kāśyapa,
it is with a person who does not uphold the precepts yet wears the kāṣāya robe.
For example, just as the son of a householder bathes himself thoroughly, puts on pure white garments, and wears a garland of *campaka* flowers;
so too, Kāśyapa, is it with one who is learned and maintains the precepts when they don the saffron robe.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
there are four types of those who do not uphold the precepts yet appear as if they do uphold them. What are these four?

If there is a bhikṣu who upholds the prohibitive precepts and accomplishes dignified deportment, who feels awe even toward the most minute matters, who maintains the pure precepts of a bhikṣu and perfects dignified deportment and etiquette, and whose conduct of body, speech, and mind is upright and pure, yet still calculates in terms of "self"—this, Kāśyapa, is called...
[the first type of person].
First, one who does not uphold the precepts yet appears as if upholding them.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, there is a bhikṣu who recites the Vinaya with thorough mastery, examines and abides by the laws of the Vinaya, yet does not sever the view of a self-existent body;
this is what is meant. Kāśyapa!
Second, those who do not uphold the precepts yet appear as if they do.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, there are bhikṣus who practice loving-kindness toward sentient beings and hear the teaching that all dharmas neither arise nor cease, yet they harbor fear. This, Kāśyapa, is called... [the second].
Third, not observing the precepts while appearing as if one observes them.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, when a bhikṣu practices the twelve dharmas of pure meritorious conduct, yet gives rise to the view that "I exist" and "mine exists," this is called [the third]. Kāśyapa!
Fourth, there is the non-observance of precepts that appears as if it were the observance of precepts.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa:

that which is called the "observance of precepts" means being without self and without what belongs to a self, without action and without non-action, and without phenomenon and without non-phenomenon.

Furthermore, there is neither deportment nor conduct, neither acting nor not acting; there is no characteristic of name-and-form, nor is there any non-characteristic; there is neither cessation nor non-cessation; there is neither grasping nor relinquishing, and there is nothing that can be grasped nor anything that cannot be relinquished.
One does not designate "sentient beings," nor does one designate "the absence of sentient beings.
There is no verbal activity and no non-verbal activity; there is no mind and no non-mind; there is no reliance and no non-reliance; there is no precept and no non-precept. This, Kāśyapa, is called—
"The untainted noble precepts do not fall into any state; they transcend the three realms and are free from all attachments.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Holding the precepts, one has neither existence nor defilement; Holding the precepts, one is without pride and does not rely [on anything]."
Upholding the precepts, one is neither obscured nor bound; upholding the precepts, one is free from dust and defilement.
Ultimately at rest in unsurpassed tranquility, without thought or non-thought, and likewise without impurity;
all lamentation and all dependencies are severed—this, Kāśyapa, is upholding the Buddha’s precepts.
Not attached to body or speech, not relying on life, Not craving anything, one undergoes birth and death;
With rightness in coming, going, and staying, one dwells in the true path— This, Kāśyapa, is upholding the Buddha’s precepts.
Not attached to the world, not relying on the world, Attaining clarity, without darkness, without anything existing;
Without the notion of self, without the notion of other, Severing all notions to attain purity;
Without this shore, that shore, or anything in between, One is likewise unattached to this shore or that shore.
Without bondage, without deceit, and free from all outflows—this, Kāśyapa, is upholding the Buddha’s precepts.
Not clinging with mind to name or form, with meditative concentration and right mindfulness taming the heart;
being without self and without "mine"—this, Kāśyapa, is called abiding in the precepts.
One attains liberation not by relying on prohibitive precepts, nor does one take joy in merely observing them;
seeking the Eightfold Noble Path beyond this—this is called the mark of pure ethical discipline.
Not expecting to maintain the precepts nor relying on meditative concentration, yet claiming that by practicing this one attains wisdom—
this state of neither having nor attaining is the noble nature, the pure noble precepts praised by the Buddha.
Having realized that the view of a self-body is liberation of mind, one never gives rise to "I" or "mine";
with a mind able to understand emptiness, the realm of the Buddha—such upholding of the precepts is unsurpassed.
Abiding well in pure precepts, one attains meditative concentration; having attained meditative concentration, one cultivates wisdom;
having cultivated wisdom, one then attains liberation; having reached liberation, one attains the equality of the precepts.
When he had spoken this verse, eight hundred bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya), and thirty-two thousand people attained the dust-free, stainless Dharma-eye.
Five hundred bhikṣus who had previously attained meditative concentration were unable to comprehend this profound teaching as the Buddha spoke it; they rose from their seats and departed.
Thereupon, Mahākāśyapa addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"These five hundred bhikṣus had previously attained meditative concentration; however, upon hearing this profound Dharma, they were unable to comprehend it and immediately rose and departed."
The World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying:
“Because these five hundred bhikṣus are arrogant and conceited, they are unable to understand this untainted pure precept.

The Dharma that has been taught is exceedingly profound and subtle; the Way of the Buddhas is supremely profound and wondrous. It cannot be understood by those who have not planted roots of goodness or who associate with evil friends.”
These five hundred bhikṣus were, in the past when the Tathāgata Kāśyapa appeared in the world, all disciples of non-Buddhist teachers.
When they heard the Tathāgata Kāśyapa preaching the Dharma, because they clung to views regarding existence, their minds attained joy upon hearing the teaching for the first time.
By these causes and conditions, when his body perished and his life ended, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
When his life there ended, he returned to the human world and left the household life to study the Path within my Dharma.

These bhikṣus have been impaired by their views; though they hear this profound Dharma, they cannot comprehend it. Now, having begun to create the necessary conditions, they will no longer be reborn in the evil realms, and upon the end of this present life, they shall attain parinirvāṇa.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"Go and transform those five hundred bhikṣus.
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
"O World-Honored One!
These five hundred bhikṣus do not accept the Buddha's teaching; how much less would I?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One manifested a transformed bhikṣu on that path.
Having seen this, five hundred bhikṣus went to where the transformed bhikṣu was and asked him,
"Venerable ones!
Where do you intend to go?"
The transformed bhikṣu said:
"I wish to go to the mountains and marshes to dwell in peace and happiness. Why is this?"
"Because I could not understand the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One which I have just heard," he then said,
"Virtuous ones!..."
"We too have heard the World-Honored One preach the Dharma, yet we cannot understand it and are filled with fear; we wish to go to the mountains and marshes to dwell in peace and happiness.
The transformed bhikṣus said, "Virtuous ones!..."
Come now, let us deliberate together with sincerity; do not engage in dispute, for that is not the Dharma of a śramaṇa.
Venerable friends!
When one speaks of parinirvāṇa, by what kind of dharma does one attain parinirvāṇa?
Within this body, what is a sentient being?
What is a self, a person, or a life-span?
Regarding parinirvāṇa, by the exhaustion of which phenomena does one attain parinirvāṇa?
The five hundred bhikṣus said,
"When lust, anger, and delusion are exhausted, one attains parinirvāṇa.
The transformed bhikṣu asked:
"Venerable friends!
Is there such a thing as the total exhaustion of lust, anger, and delusion?
And yet it is said that through this exhaustion one attains parinirvāṇa."
The five hundred bhikṣus replied:
"Venerable sirs!
Lust, anger, and delusion do not exist within, nor do they exist without, nor do they exist in between the two; yet they are not non-existent either."
The transformed bhikṣu said:
"Therefore, worthy ones!
You should not engage in discursive thought, nor should you engage in contrary thought."
If one neither thinks nor reflects, then there is neither defilement nor non-defilement.
That which is neither defiled nor non-defiled is called tranquility and stillness.

You venerable ones should know that the aggregate of morality is neither born nor does it enter parinirvāṇa; likewise, the aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation are neither born nor do they enter parinirvāṇa.
Venerable friends!
It is because of this fivefold dharma-body that Nirvana is so described; this dharma is remote, empty, and non-existent, without grasping and without cessation.
Thus it is, worthy ones!
How could one conceive of parinirvāṇa?
For this reason, worthy ones!
Do not conceive of conception, nor conceive of non-conception; furthermore, do not sever conception or non-conception, for to sever conception and non-conception constitutes a great condition.
"Venerable friends!
If one enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, it appears as though there is something being done.
When this Dharma was spoken, the outflows of five hundred bhikṣus were forever exhausted, and their minds attained liberation.
He then went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Thereupon, the Venerable Subhūti asked the bhikṣus:
"Virtuous ones, where have you been just now?"
"From where have you come now?
The bhikṣus said, "Venerable Subhūti!"
“The Dharma taught by the Buddha neither goes nor comes.
Subhūti then asked the venerable ones: “Who is your teacher?”
The bhikṣus replied,
"It is said that non-arising and non-ceasing are [the dharmadhātu]. Subhūti asked again:
"How does one know the Dharma? He replied:
"Without bondage and without liberation."
Subhūti asked again: "Virtuous ones!
How is there liberation?"
He replied, "Ignorance ceases and clarity arises. Subhūti asked again:
"Virtuous ones! Who is your disciple? They replied:
"It means that one attains such-and-such right knowledge.
Subhūti asked again: "Venerable sirs!"
"When will he enter parinirvāṇa?
He replied: "He will enter parinirvāṇa as a transformation of the Tathāgata."
Subhūti asked again: "Venerable ones!
Have you completed what was to be done?"
He replied, "I have completely severed all that is 'mine' and all that is 'I'.
Subhūti asked again:
"Virtuous ones! Who are your fellow practitioners of the holy life? They replied:
“They do not course within the three realms.
Subhūti asked again: “Venerable sirs! [How so?]”
"Are the fetters exhausted?
He replied, "All dharmas have reached ultimate cessation."
Subhūti asked again: "Venerable sirs!
Have you subdued Māra?"
He replied, "The aggregates (skandhas) cannot be apprehended.
Subhūti asked again:
"Venerable friends!
Are you following the instructions of the Honored One? They replied:
“There is no body, speech, or mind.
Subhūti asked again: “Venerable friends!”
"Is it a pure field of merit?
He replied, "There is no recipient, nor is there anything received."
Subhūti asked again: "Virtuous ones!
Have you crossed over birth and death?"
He replied, "It is neither impermanent nor eternal. Subhūti asked again:
"Venerable friends!
Are you heading toward the field of merit? They replied:
"All attachments have been completely liberated.
Subhūti asked again: "Virtuous ones!..."
"To where do they go?
He replied, "They follow wherever the Tathāgata transforms them."
Thus, when the Venerable Subhūti had asked and the five hundred bhikṣus had answered,

the great assembly, having heard this, attained liberation of mind through the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*)— eight hundred bhikṣus did so— and the dust-free, stainless Dharma-eye arose in thirty-two thousand people.
Thereupon, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One, saying:
“How marvelous, how extraordinary!
This Jewel-Adornment Sūtra brings great benefit and inspires sons and daughters of noble family who are intent upon the Mahāyāna.”
Subhūti again asked the World-Honored One:
"How much merit will those sons and daughters of good family obtain who preach this Jewel-Adorned Sūtra?"
The World-Honored One replied:

"If sons or daughters of noble family teach this *Ratnavyūha Sūtra* to others, or transcribe its scrolls wherever they are kept, that place shall become the most wondrous stupa and temple in all the heavens and upon earth."
If one hears [this teaching] from a Dharma Master, upholds it, recites it, and copies it into a scroll, one should revere that Dharma Master as if he were the Tathāgata.

If one reveres the Dharma Master and makes offerings to him with devotion, I declare that such a person will certainly attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path; at the time of their death, they will surely behold the Tathāgata, and this person shall obtain ten kinds of purity of body.
What are the ten?
First, at the time of death, one is joyful and without weariness;
second, the eyes are not distracted.
Third, the hands are not disturbed;
fourth, the mind is not disturbed;
fifth, the body is not troubled.
Sixth, not losing the great or small impurities;
seventh, the mind is not defiled;
eighth, the mind is not distracted or confused.
Ninth, one does not touch empty space with the hands;
tenth, one passes away while remaining seated.
These are called the ten kinds of bodily purity.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
one shall attain ten kinds of purity of speech.
What are these ten?
First, the excellent voice;
second, the gentle voice;
third, the pleasant voice.
Fourth, the voice of affection;
fifth, the gentle and supple voice;
sixth, the unimpeded voice;
Seventh, the honored voice;
eighth, the receptive voice;
ninth, the voice received by the devas;
Tenth is the sound received by the Buddha.
These are called the ten kinds of purity of speech.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
One shall attain ten kinds of purity of mind.
What are these ten? First, being without resentment, one does not become angry with others.
Second, being without resentment and not speaking [of others' faults];
third, not seeking out shortcomings;
fourth, being free from fetters.
Fifth, being free from perverted perceptions;
sixth, having no indolence in the mind;
seventh, not being negligent regarding the precepts.
Eighth, receiving the joy of giving with a pure intention;
ninth, being free from arrogance and pride;
tenth, attaining samādhi and obtaining all Buddha-dharmas.
These are the ten kinds of purity of mind!

"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, suppose there were as many lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, filled with the seven treasures, and one were to make offerings to as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their assemblies of disciples as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, providing all manner of gifts and comforts for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, and even after their parinirvāṇa, erecting stupas made of the seven treasures; [if one were to do this, it would not equal the merit of one who attains purity of mind]."
It is not as good as when sons or daughters of good family hear this *Ratnavyūha Sūtra*, receive and uphold it, recite it, explain it to others, and do not slander it.
If there is a woman who speaks this sutra, that woman shall never fall into the evil realms, nor shall she ever again receive a female body.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!

If there are members of any clan who wish to offer all manner of rare and exquisite offerings to this sutra, they should receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and explain the scroll to others; this constitutes having already made offerings to this sutra.
"If there are those who receive, uphold, recite, transcribe, or explain it to others, they shall thereby be making offerings to all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.

When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, along with all the devas, nāgas, spirits, and the people of the world, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Precious Adornment Spoken by the Buddha.
